source_user: A service receives a mix of short prompts and long generations. Design an evaluation plan that reports TTFT, TPOT, throughput, queueing, and P99 latency. Scenario variant 247: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: separate prefill and decode behavior; fix workload distribution; report warmup; use repeated trials; capture GPU memory and request-level traces.
corrected_answer:
Scope and assumptions (variant 1247, framing: System Design). Assume a decoder-only LLM served by a continuous-batching engine (vLLM / TensorRT-LLM class) with paged KV cache, fixed tensor-parallel degree, homogeneous GPUs, and a single pinned model+engine build for the entire study. Traffic is bimodal: short prompts (~128-512 input tokens) with long generations (~512-2048 output tokens), interleaved with short-in/short-out requests. All numeric targets below are estimates to be measured on the target cluster, not platform facts. Metric definitions are fixed up front: TTFT = client send -> first streamed token; TPOT = (end-to-end - TTFT) / (output_tokens - 1); throughput reported separately as output tok/s and requests/s; queueing = engine-side wait before first scheduler admission; P99 computed per workload class, never pooled across classes.

Mechanism. TTFT decomposes into queue wait + scheduling delay + prefill compute; prefill is compute-bound and scales with total prefilled tokens, with a superlinear attention term at long context. TPOT is the steady-state decode step time, dominated by HBM bandwidth for weight and KV reads, so it degrades as concurrent batch size and accumulated KV length grow. Throughput rises with batch size until KV-cache blocks or memory bandwidth saturate; past that knee, added load converts directly into queueing and P99 tail. Because prefill and decode live in different regimes, any single pooled average latency number is uninterpretable and must be rejected as a reporting artifact.

Falsifiable hypothesis (controlled experiment centers on chunked prefill token budget). H1: enabling chunked prefill with a per-step token budget of ~2048 tokens reduces decode-phase TPOT p99 by >=20% at 80% of saturation load, while increasing mean TTFT by <=15%. Null hypothesis: the observed effect lies inside the noise band, defined as the 95% CI half-width of the baseline arm across repeated trials.

Experiment design. Arms: baseline scheduler vs chunked prefill. Sweep the token budget over {512, 1024, 2048, 4096} in a second pass only if H1 is not rejected, so the primary test stays a single pre-registered comparison. Everything else is held fixed: model weights, engine build, GPU SKU and count, driver/NCCL versions, sampling parameters, and the replayed request trace including arrival timestamps. Randomize arm order across trials to absorb drift in the shared environment.

Measurement protocol. Open-loop load generator with Poisson arrivals; per-request trace records arrival, admission, first token, per-token timestamps, input/output token counts, and workload class. Discard a warmup window (first 3 minutes or until the running throughput mean is stable within 2% over 60s, whichever is later), then hold a 15-minute measurement window. Five independent trials per arm with engine restart between trials to avoid carry-over of cache state; report median with the 5th/95th trial spread, and bootstrap 95% CIs for p99. Sample GPU memory, SM utilization, achieved HBM bandwidth, KV-block occupancy, preemption count, and NCCL/NIC counters at 1s resolution alongside the request trace.

Confounders to control explicitly: warmup and JIT/graph-capture effects; prompt-mix drift between arms (freeze a replayed trace, do not resample); tokenizer differences inflating token counts; client-side bottlenecks (verify the generator can exceed the target rate against a null endpoint); GPU clock throttling (log nvidia-smi clocks and temperature, drop trials with thermal or power capping); other tenants on the node or fabric; and autoscaling or router changes mid-run.

Rollback criteria and gates. Promote the treatment only if the pre-registered effect size holds with a 95% CI excluding the null, error rate stays <=0.1%, no OOM or engine restart occurs across all trials, and quality on the held-out eval is unchanged within tolerance. Roll back immediately if P99 end-to-end for any workload class regresses >10%, preemption/recompute exceeds 1% of requests, or the error rate exceeds 0.5% during a canary at 10% traffic. Canary for at least one full diurnal cycle before fleet-wide rollout; keep the previous engine build resident so rollback is a router flip, not a redeploy.

What would falsify this plan itself: if TTFT and TPOT move together in every arm, the prefill/decode decomposition is not capturing the real bottleneck, and the next step is kernel-level profiling (Nsight Systems) plus a roofline check rather than more scheduler tuning.
risks: Pooling short-prompt and long-generation classes into one P99 hides the regression that matters.
Closed-loop or under-provisioned load generators understate queueing and cap measured throughput.
Tuning for throughput at high KV utilization can trigger preemption/recompute storms that show up only at the tail.
Cross-tenant GPU or fabric contention is attributed to the treatment when it is environmental.
evidence_required: Per-request traces with arrival, admission, first-token and per-token timestamps, plus input/output token counts and class labels.
Engine metrics: KV-block occupancy, running/waiting batch sizes, preemption and recomputed-token counters.
GPU telemetry at 1s resolution: memory, SM utilization, achieved HBM bandwidth, clocks, power and thermal capping flags.
Version manifest: model hash, engine build, CUDA/driver/NCCL versions, and the exact scheduler flags per arm.
Held-out quality eval results from the same build used for the performance run.
